title: The Nightmare by Fuseli: the demon, the horse and the woman he could not forget
question: A demon on her chest, a horse at the curtain, and a portrait hidden on the back. Whose nightmare is this?

seo.meta_title: The Nightmare by Fuseli: Meaning, Story and Hidden Details
seo.meta_description: A guided zoom through Fuseli's The Nightmare (1781): the incubus, the blind-eyed horse, the objects by the bed and the portrait hidden on the back.

intro: The Nightmare is a painting by the Swiss-born artist Henry Fuseli from 1781, now in the Detroit Institute of Arts. A young woman lies asleep, flung across her bed with her head hanging down. On her chest crouches a demon, an incubus, staring out at the viewer, while a horse's head with blank, pupil-less eyes pushes through the red curtains. Shown in London in 1782, it shocked visitors and made Fuseli famous.

sections.heading: London, 1782
paragraphs: Fuseli, born Johann Heinrich Füssli in Zürich, showed The Nightmare at the Royal Academy in London in 1782. Visitors were startled, and some critics were scandalised, but it became his first commercial success. The painting itself sold for twenty guineas.
The real money was in the print. Thomas Burke's engraving went on sale in January 1783 and spread so widely that it earned the publisher, John Raphael Smith, more than 500 pounds.

sections.heading: What a "nightmare" used to mean
paragraphs: In Fuseli's time, a nightmare was not just a bad dream. The word described a whole experience: a weight on the chest, difficulty breathing, dread and being unable to move. Today we would call much of it sleep paralysis.

The "mare" in nightmare does not come from the horse. It comes from mara, a spirit of Scandinavian folklore that sat on sleepers and suffocated them. Fuseli painted both: the spirit on her chest, and, as a visual pun, the mare at the curtain.

sections.heading: Anna
paragraphs: In Zürich, Fuseli had fallen in love with Anna Landolt, the niece of his friend, the writer Johann Kaspar Lavater. In 1779 he wrote to Lavater about his fantasies of her. Her father refused his proposal, and she soon married someone else.

On the back of the canvas of The Nightmare is an unfinished portrait of a young woman, which may be Anna. The art historian H. W. Janson suggested that the sleeper is Anna and the demon is Fuseli himself. It is a theory, but a hard one to forget once you have heard it.

sections.heading: Copies, parodies and Frankenstein
paragraphs: Fuseli painted at least three more versions; the most important, from around 1790 to 1791, is in the Goethe Museum in Frankfurt. Satirists like Thomas Rowlandson and George Cruikshank borrowed the composition to mock politicians.

Writers borrowed it too. The scene in Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) where the creature's victim lies thrown across her bed seems to echo it, and Edgar Allan Poe's The Fall of the House of Usher speaks of "an incubus of utterly causeless alarm". Carl Jung reproduced the painting in Man and His Symbols (1964).

meaning: Fuseli left no explanation, and readings have multiplied.

One is medical and folkloric: a picture of what people in the 18th century believed happened in a nightmare. Another is erotic: many critics have read the incubus and the intruding horse as images of desire, and the woman's pose as sexual rather than simply asleep. A third is personal, through Anna Landolt and the portrait on the back.
The painting refuses to choose, which is partly why it still works. It shows the moment between sleep and waking, when you cannot tell what is real.
whereToSee: Detroit Institute of Arts, Detroit, Michigan. A later version (c. 1790-91) is in the Goethe Museum (Frankfurter Goethe-Haus) in Frankfurt.

details.headline: London, 1782
details.text: The Royal Academy opens its doors, and visitors stop in front of this painting, shocked. Let's see what they saw.

details.headline: A woman asleep
details.text: She lies across the end of the bed in a white gown, arms thrown back. Deep asleep. Or is she?

details.headline: Head hanging down
details.text: Her head drops over the edge of the bed, exposing her long neck. People believed this position brought on nightmares.

details.headline: A hand touching the floor
details.text: Her arm hangs all the way down; the fingertips barely touch the floor. A dark bracelet on her wrist is the only thing holding her to the waking world.

details.headline: But she's not alone
details.text: A demon crouches on her chest, heavy and squat. This is the incubus, the weight that sleepers felt and could not throw off.

details.headline: He is looking at you
details.text: Look at his face: ape-like, grinning, turned not towards her but straight out of the painting, at us.

details.headline: And then, through the curtain
details.text: On the left, a horse's head pushes through a gap in the red velvet curtains. A preliminary sketch has no horse: Fuseli probably added it late.

details.headline: Eyes without pupils
details.text: Its eyes are blank and white, with no pupils at all. Of everything in the room, it is the strangest.

details.headline: It's not about the horse
details.text: The "mare" in nightmare comes from mara, a spirit that sat on sleepers and suffocated them. Fuseli painted the spirit, and added a horse as a pun.

details.headline: By the bed
details.text: On a little round table: a mirror, a glass phial and a book. Ordinary bedside things, in a room where nothing is ordinary.

details.headline: Silk in the dark
details.text: Under her, a tangle of yellow and red drapery glows against the darkness, the only warm colour in the room.

details.headline: Is the demon the painter?
details.text: One art historian thought so. Fuseli loved a young woman, Anna Landolt. She never loved him back, and on the back of this canvas is a portrait that may be her.
